title: How to Avoid Common TOK Exhibition Mistakes
summary: Learn how to avoid common TOK exhibition mistakes, choose effective objects, write focused commentary, and use the September-November term wisely.
body_markdown:
The best way to **avoid common TOK exhibition mistakes** is to keep the official assessment task at the centre of every decision. Choose one prescribed prompt, use three specific objects with identifiable real-world contexts, and explain what each object uniquely reveals about the prompt.


This matters during the **IB TOK fall term** , when many students progress from planning to object approval and commentary drafting. The September-November period provides time to test ideas, replace unsuitable objects, use permitted teacher feedback, and revise carefully.


### Confirm the TOK exhibition requirements first


The TOK exhibition explores how TOK manifests in the world around us. According to the[official IB TOK subject brief](https://ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/dp/pdfs/tok-sb-english.pdf) , it is internally assessed, externally moderated, and worth **one-third of the TOK result** .


Your submitted work must contain:


- **One prescribed IA prompt** from the official list of 35
- **Three objects** , or images of objects, connected to that prompt
- A **specific real-world context** for each object
- Commentary explaining and justifying each object’s connection
- Appropriate citations and references
- No more than **950 words across all three commentaries**


The limit is a combined maximum, not 950 words per object. Reproduce the prompt accurately from the current materials supplied by your school rather than relying on memory or an unofficial paraphrase.


### Mistake 1: Treating the prompt as a broad topic


A prescribed prompt is a knowledge question, not a topic label. “Who owns knowledge?” does not simply invite a description of copyright, while “What counts as good evidence for a claim?” does not ask for a list of evidence types.


Underline the prompt’s decisive words and write a provisional one-sentence answer. For example: “What counts as good evidence depends partly on the methods and standards of the community evaluating the claim.” This answer can change, but it gives the exhibition direction.


Use a reliable[guide to all 35 TOK exhibition prompts](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/tok-exhibition-prompts-b4a14cd7) during planning, while retaining the official wording in your final submission.


### Mistake 2: Choosing generic or invented objects


An object must be a particular item in an identifiable context. “A newspaper,” “a calculator,” or “a religious text” describes a category, not a specific object.


Stronger choices include a named article published on a particular date, the calculator used during a documented classroom activity, or an annotated edition used within a named community. Digital objects are acceptable when you identify the exact post, screenshot, webpage, recording, or document and establish where and when it existed.


Avoid manufacturing a symbolic object solely for the exhibition. A collage created to represent bias is harder to justify than a pre-existing campaign poster with a traceable producer and audience. The IB’s[activity on AI-generated content as a TOK object](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/tok-activity-using-ai-generated-content-as-a-tok-object-en.pdf) demonstrates how contemporary digital material can support TOK analysis when its context is examined carefully.


Test candidates with the[RevisionDojo object-selection checklist](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/selecting-the-right-objects-for-your-tok-exhibition) .


### Mistake 3: Describing instead of analysing knowledge


Students often use too many words recounting an object’s history or appearance. Context matters only when it helps establish the connection to the prompt.


Each object section should perform five jobs:


Step Question to answer


Identify What exactly is the object?


Contextualise Who produced or used it, where, when, and why?


Connect How does it relate to the prompt’s exact wording?


Analyse What does it reveal about knowledge?


Justify Why does it make a distinct contribution?


Identifying a corrected laboratory report provides context. TOK analysis begins when you explain how its corrections show that scientific reliability depends on transparent methods, checking, and a community’s willingness to revise claims.


The[commentary planning guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-create-an-engaging-tok-exhibition-commentary) can help separate necessary context from genuine analysis.


### Mistake 4: Leaving the prompt connection implicit


A reader should not have to infer why an object belongs. State a direct claim, such as: “This object suggests that evidence becomes persuasive only when its method of production can be examined.” Support it with relevant details from the object’s context.


Replace your prompt temporarily with another prescribed prompt. If the commentary still works almost unchanged, your reasoning is probably too generic. Use key words from the chosen prompt naturally, but always explain their significance.


### Mistake 5: Repeating the same point three times


Three objects do not automatically create three perspectives. Three articles about misinformation may illustrate the same problem and leave the exhibition conceptually narrow.


Give each object a distinct role:


- **Object 1:** establishes a plausible answer
- **Object 2:** complicates it through uncertainty, bias, or disagreement
- **Object 3:** introduces another community, method, culture, period, or area of knowledge


The objects need not contradict one another. They should form one coherent exploration without repeating the same argument. Reviewing selected[TOK exhibition exemplars](https://www.revisiondojo.com/coursework-exemplars/tok-exhibition/sl) can clarify the difference between conceptual variety and superficial variety.


### Mistake 6: Using vocabulary without TOK thinking


Terms such as **perspective** , **evidence** , **authority** , and **interpretation** help only when applied precisely. Instead of writing “This relates to perspective,” identify whose perspective matters, how it formed, what it excludes, and how that affects a knowledge claim.


One well-developed concept per object is usually stronger than several unexplained terms. TOK vocabulary should make the reasoning more exact, not merely make the commentary sound academic.


### Mistake 7: Neglecting evidence and references


Factual claims about an object’s creator, history, publication, use, or controversy require support. Cite borrowed images and acknowledge relevant research.


If you photograph a personal object, identify it and provide enough context to explain its significance. Do not move analysis into footnotes to avoid the word limit, since references should document sources rather than carry the argument. The[RevisionDojo exhibition administration notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-theory-of-knowledge-tok/ib-theory-of-knowledge-tok-29-the-exhibition-event-and-the-administra-92217/notes) explain practical expectations concerning images, identification, and references.


### A practical September-November TOK schedule


Schools set their own deadlines, so confirm yours first. This schedule is advice, not an IB requirement.


Period Main task Evidence of progress


September Compare prompts and brainstorm objects Strong prompt shortlist and at least five possible objects


Early October Confirm the prompt and objects One context statement and knowledge claim per object


Late October Draft all commentaries Complete draft close to 950 words


November Revise, reference, and proofread Accurate prompt, images, citations, and word count


Test whether objects can sustain analysis before polishing prose. The[step-by-step TOK exhibition guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-excel-in-your-ib-tok-exhibition-complete-step-by-step-guide) can turn these stages into manageable weekly tasks.


### Final submission checklist


Before submitting, confirm that:


- The prescribed prompt is copied exactly.
- All three objects have specific real-world contexts.
- Every prompt connection is explicit.
- Each object contributes a different insight.
- Analysis outweighs description.
- Images, factual claims, and borrowed ideas are referenced.
- The combined commentary is no more than **950 words** .
- The work remains recognizably your own.


RevisionDojo’s[exhibition-at-a-glance notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-theory-of-knowledge-tok/ib-theory-of-knowledge-tok-21-the-exhibition-at-a-glance/notes) provide a useful final check.


### Conclusion


To avoid common TOK exhibition mistakes, prioritize specific objects, explicit prompt links, knowledge analysis, distinct contributions, and accurate referencing. The exhibition is not a display of three interesting items; it explains how knowledge operates in concrete real-world contexts.


A disciplined fall schedule lets you replace weak objects before they produce weak commentary. RevisionDojo’s TOK resources and Jojo AI can support planning and self-questioning, but the final reasoning and writing must remain your own.
